rows.why: Only documents change (the instructions Tasks follow are other kinds), so a recheck by another runner reads that the diff is documents and inside the PBI before the merge, and a revert restores them.
Words that must not be published are copied by readers and mirrors once they are on main.

A recheck installs the head's bun.lock without lifecycle scripts, checks the licenses and lists every changed entry (version, source, integrity) before the merge; other lock files fail the recheck and are asked. A revert restores the lock, but what an install already ran stays.
Workflow and repository settings run with the repository's credentials as soon as they are merged.
The gate itself decides what is asked, so a bad change here weakens the check on every later merge.
Host scripts run as root from main on every start; a revert comes after the first run.
A large diff can be reverted as a whole, and a recheck reads it again before the merge.
Instruction files change what Tasks do next, but a revert restores them and a recheck reads the scope first.
The schema only grows, so a migration is undone by a later one, and traces of the run remain.
The rollback path itself is rechecked before the merge; a bad change is undone from the release tag.
The rules are text in the repository; a revert restores them and a recheck reads the change first.
A sent comment can be edited or deleted, but notifications and the edit history remain.
No snapshot is taken of its own; an undo is a later migration and the earlier data shape is gone.
The candidate is boot-checked first and the daemon rolls back by itself; the rescue page undoes it.
They run as root from main on every start, so a bad script has run before it can be stopped.
